- **Snakes & Reptiles:** An extensive collection of venomous and non-venomous snakes from across the globe, including mambas, cobras, and taipans, as well as Komodo dragons and giant tortoises.
- **Alligators & Crocodiles:** Enclosures featuring massive saltwater and American alligators, along with alligator-wrestling demonstrations.
- **Interactive Shows:** Regularly scheduled educational and interactive presentations, including snake shows, alligator/crocodile shows, and bird shows.
- **Botanical Displays:** Impeccably landscaped outdoor gardens featuring thousands of flowers, geological displays, and an Old West-themed area.

It's **La Bufadora**, a blowhole at the end of the Punta Banda peninsula in Baja California, Mexico. It's about 27 km (17 mi) south of Ensenada, according to [Wikipedia](w6), and the drive takes roughly 30 minutes.

Waves push air and water into a sea cave at the base of the cliff. The water then blasts upward through the opening. [Luggage & Lipstick](w3) says the spray can reach about 100 feet, and it often lands on the viewing ledge. Other sources give lower heights. [Forever Karen](w2) says 60 feet.

The "second-largest" claim comes from travel blogs. [Forever Karen](w1) says the largest is in Oahu, and calls La Bufadora the second-largest in North America. Other pages say second-largest in the world, so I couldn't pin down which wording is right.

[Forever Karen](w5) says it's most impressive at high tide. A busy market of crafts and street food sits next to the viewpoint.

La Bufadora is a natural blowhole and marine geyser where powerful ocean waves crash into an underwater sea cave, forcing water up through a narrow opening in the cliff face. This creates spectacular water spouts that can shoot up to 60–100 feet (18–30 meters) into the air, accompanied by a distinctive roaring sound. It is widely recognized as the **second-largest marine geyser in the world** (or sometimes cited as the largest in North America).

The site is easily accessible via a cliffside boardwalk that offers panoramic views of the Pacific Ocean and the dramatic coastal cliffs. It's best visited during high tide when the waves are strongest, and it's a popular stop for tourists exploring the Ensenada area.
